title: Can AI create a set of SSDD Problems?
author: Craig Barton
summary: Craig Barton tests whether ChatGPT can write Same Surface, Different Deep (SSDD) problem sets, four questions that look alike but come from different areas of maths. He explains why the format works, linking it to retrieval practice, attention and discriminative contrast in interleaving, then shares his prompt and three outputs with candid verdicts. The first set is decent, the second weak because a shared number gives little to think about, and a revised prompt improves the third. He notes ChatGPT's habits, such as always putting the named topic first and favouring equation questions. His conclusion is that AI is a good generator of seeds that teachers must edit, and that vague prompts reveal the writer's own unstated assumptions.
points: SSDD sets build the skill of recognising which topic a question belongs to, rather than launching into a habitual procedure.
ChatGPT produces usable draft sets, but it has predictable biases, such as placing the stated topic first and over-using equation questions.
Feedback to the model on ordering, variety and surface similarity noticeably improved the second round of output.
Editing a draft takes seconds compared with writing a set from scratch, so AI helps teachers work faster and, with oversight, better.
AI cannot substitute for teacher expertise, and refining prompts exposes the unstated assumptions in one's own thinking.
quotes: I love these sets of problems because they help students develop a key problem-solving skill: recognising what topic a question is from. Students need to sift through the constant surface features to figure out what the question is asking them to do, instead of just launching into the same procedure every time they see a trapezium or a fraction.

SSDD Problems are great to use after you have finished teaching a topic. As long as one of the questions in the set of four relates to that topic and the other questions relate to concepts students have encountered, you have a supercharged, interleaved resource.

A pretty good effort! I expected it to just come up with procedural questions with the operation changed (3/4 + 1/2, 3/4 x 1/2, etc), but the fact it has wrapped these questions up in a context increases the challenge. Question 3 is significantly more straightforward than the other 3, but that is not a bad thing.

This is better, although I think using dimensions 15, 2, and 3 in Question 3 would have improved the challenge of discriminative contrast with Question 2. Likewise, those three numbers could have been included in Question 4.
ChatGPT is good at creating the seeds of a set of SSDD Problems. Whilst no set is perfect, it is undoubtedly good at generating ideas for topics to include, and questions to assess those topics.

If someone with no experience writing SSDD Problems relied solely on the output of my prompts, the results would not be great. AIs, in their current form, are best used to generate ideas and suggest improvements—they cannot substitute for teacher experience or expertise.

Looking back at my original prompt, I can see why ChatGPT produced the second set of questions—my unstated assumptions were to blame. If these models do not produce the output we have in mind, the fault is likely to rest on us.
